analysis.one_liner: Makes gun trafficking—buying guns for people barred from owning them—a federal crime.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 84 cosponsors, it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee for nearly two years until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new federal crime of firearms trafficking: buying or transferring a gun intending to hand it to someone legally barred from owning one, lying on the required firearms paperwork, or helping someone else do those things. Penalties run up to 20 years in prison, more for organizers, plus up to 10 years for conspiracies. Lawful gifts and inheritance transfers would be exempt. The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which sent it to a crime subcommittee, and no action ever followed.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, communities affected by illegal gun violence would gain a tool prosecutors currently lack: a specific federal trafficking charge aimed at straw purchasers and the people who run them, rather than relying on a patchwork of paperwork violations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities hit by illegal gun trafficking

how_it_helps.text: It creates a dedicated federal crime for buying a gun with the intent to deliver it to someone prohibited by federal or state law from possessing one, punishable by up to 20 years in prison and up to 25 for an organizer running a group of five or more people.
It criminalizes lying or giving false material information on the ATF firearms transaction record, the form used at purchase, closing a common loophole in how straw purchases are prosecuted.
It reaches the people behind the scheme, not just the buyer, by penalizing anyone who knowingly directs, promotes, or facilitates the prohibited conduct, and by adding up to 10 years for conspiracy.
It directs the U.S. Sentencing Commission to review whether the existing penalty structure for trafficking cases, based on the number of guns involved, reflects the seriousness of the offense.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on gun traffickers and straw purchasers facing up to 20 years in prison, on prosecutors and the court system handling new cases, and modestly on gun sellers, who would need to be careful about transfers to people they have reason to believe are prohibited buyers.

drawbacks.text: The standard of 'reasonable cause to believe' the recipient is prohibited could sweep in sellers who did not actually know, raising over-criminalization concerns for otherwise lawful transfers and imposing prison terms of up to 20 years on a newly created offense.
Federal prosecutors already bring straw-purchase and false-statement cases under existing law, so the practical gain of the new crime may be smaller than its length suggests.
The gift exception only protects gifts to people not prohibited from owning guns, so legitimate-looking transfers could still trigger federal investigation even when no trafficking occurred.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people living with the effects of illegal guns flowing across state lines, a targeted federal trafficking charge with real penalties is a meaningful enforcement tool, and the bill carved out lawful gifts and inheritances. The honest costs are the over-criminalization risk from a 'reasonable cause to believe' standard and the prison, prosecutorial, and court resources a new 20-year offense consumes. On balance it is a narrowly drawn enforcement bill with modest downsides, but its value depends entirely on how prosecutors use it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which sent it to its crime subcommittee on March 21, 2017, and it sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no path to the floor for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Representative Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on March 9, 2017, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Elijah Cummings, Peter King, Daniel Meehan, Robin Kelly, and Daniel Donovan.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, the committee that controls whether it ever reaches the floor.
On March 21, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations, a common place for bills to go without further action.
The bill drew 84 cosponsors, 81 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but no committee or subcommittee vote was ever held, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, there is still no dedicated federal gun-trafficking crime, so the status quo holds for gun traffickers and straw purchasers, and no new enforcement burden falls on firearms sellers. Members of Congress who preferred no new gun legislation faced no vote at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo, with no new federal gun-trafficking law

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was overwhelmingly Democratic: 81 of the 84 cosponsors were Democrats, with only 3 Republicans, though its original cosponsors included members of both parties.

industries.industry: Firearms trafficking networks and straw purchasers
industries.note: The bill would make their core activity a federal crime carrying up to 20 years, plus conspiracy penalties reaching organizers. Because their profit depends on moving guns to people barred from owning them, their interest runs directly against the communities the bill protects.

The bill does not ban any lawful sale and exempts gifts and inheritances, but the 'reasonable cause to believe' standard creates legal risk for sellers who transfer guns to buyers they should have suspected were prohibited. Lawful dealers who follow the paperwork rules are largely unaffected.
